standard: Subscription / SaaS recurring-revenue metrics (MRR & ARR corpus)
source: ChartMogul / OpenView / SaaS Capital / SaaS metrics references (web-researched 2026-07-24)

entries.title: Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) — normalized monthly subscription revenue
entries.body: MRR is the normalized, amortized monthly revenue from all active recurring subscriptions. It is the central financial signal for a SaaS business because it strips out one-time fees, professional services, and usage overages. Formula: sum of active recurring subscription revenue for the month.

entries.title: Normalize annual/upfront payments to MRR (ACV ÷ 12)
entries.body: For annual or multi-month contracts, MRR = Annual Contract Value ÷ number of months, NOT the full cash received upfront. A customer paying $1,200/year contributes $100/month. Counting the full cash amount in the month received is the most common early-stage MRR accounting error.

entries.title: MRR movements — New, Expansion, Contraction, Churned
entries.body: Decompose MRR into four vectors: New (new customers), Expansion (upgrades/seat adds), Contraction (downgrades), Churned (cancellations). Net New MRR = New + Expansion − Contraction − Churned. Tracking the four separately reveals which part of the revenue engine is healthy.

entries.title: Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) = MRR × 12
entries.body: ARR is the annualized run-rate of recurring revenue. It is mainly useful for high-level growth tracking, investor reporting, and benchmarking. It is a point-in-time snapshot, not trailing revenue — GAAP revenue may lag or exceed ARR depending on signing timing.

entries.title: ARR as the primary SaaS valuation basis
entries.body: ARR (and its growth rate) is the metric VCs and public indices use to compare SaaS companies and set valuation multiples. Below ~$1M ARR, MRR is more practical; at $1M+ ARR, ARR becomes the standard language for fundraising and board reporting.

entries.title: Use MRR for week-to-week ops, ARR for trend/benchmarking
entries.body: ARR is slow to react because it is derived from MRR (12× the latest month). Most operating decisions should use MRR; ARR is best for year-over-year comparison and investor narrative. Never present ARR alone without churn and net retention context.

entries.title: ARPU / ARPA — Average Revenue Per User/Account
entries.body: ARPU = MRR ÷ active paying users. For B2B where customers are companies, ARPA (Average Revenue Per Account) = MRR ÷ active paying accounts is the more meaningful figure and feeds LTV calculations.

entries.title: ACV — Average Annual Contract Value (excludes one-time fees)
entries.body: ACV is the average annual value of a customer contract, excluding setup or one-time fees. Rising ACV signals upmarket movement; declining ACV may signal competitive pricing pressure or a deliberate move to smaller customers.

entries.title: CMRR — Committed MRR (forward projection)
entries.body: Committed MRR projects MRR into the future from expected or scheduled subscription changes (e.g. a communicated upcoming cancellation). It is a planning signal, not a guaranteed run-rate.

entries.title: Common MRR mistake — treating annual cash as in-period revenue
entries.body: Confusing cash received with MRR inflates numbers in strong acquisition months and hides the underlying trend. MRR must include only recurring subscription revenue, never one-time setup fees, services, or usage overages.

entries.title: Negative net churn — expansion exceeds churn (the 'holy grail')
entries.body: When expansion + reactivation MRR exceeds churned + contraction MRR, the revenue base grows even with zero new customers. This is the most capital-efficient growth model in SaaS and the strongest durability signal.

entries.title: MRR growth-rate benchmarks by stage
entries.body: SaaS Capital 2025 survey: median private B2B SaaS growth ~25% (down from 30% in 2023). Early-stage (Series A–B) often 30–50% annual ARR growth; growth-stage ($20–100M ARR) 20–40%; public/late-stage 15–25%. Use as reference, not a promise.
